More recently, Manitoba introduced The 2018 Climate and Green Plan ActManitoba’s 
Plan to Net Zero, which sets an ambitious goal for the province by 2050. As a comprehensive 
plan, it includes province-wide priorities, government action to lead the change, collaboration 
with Indigenous peoples, building the next generation of workers, and actions to take across all 
sectors. In addition to reducing and eliminating emissions, Manitoba aims at removing or 
offsetting emissions through a combination of activities that could include land and water-based 
carbon sequestration, carbon capture utilization and storage (CCUS), carbon stored building 
materials, and carbon offsets.1  will be discussed throughout this chapter. 
  
►Manitoba's provincial government has long recognized hydroelectric power as one of 
several characteristics that gives the province an advantage in its efforts to reduce GHG 
emissions. Virtually all electricity in the province is generated by hydroelectric stations operated 
by Manitoba Hydro, the province's Crown-owned monopoly electricity supplier. Opportunities 
also continue to exist for the development of wind power and more extensive use of geothermal 
energy. 
  
►The vastness of Manitoba is also viewed by its provincial government as an asset, 
providing opportunities for agriculture and forestry carbon sinks. Capitalizing on these natural 
carbon stores, Manitoba's Peatlands Stewardship Strategy includes the 2014 Peatlands 
Stewardship Act, which aims to balance responsible economic development with conservation of 
peatland ecosystems.10 The legislation is the first of its kind in Canada and builds upon the 
existing ban against peat mining in provincial parks as well as in the site east of Lake Winnipeg 
where Pimachiowin Aki, the ancestral home of the Anishinaabeg, is located and which received 
UNESCO world heritage status in 2018.11

promoting Manitoba as a source of green renewable energy supplied by current and future 
developments in hydroelectricity and, to a lesser extent, wind power.

VII. Conclusion 
8:31. Concluding Remarks 
  
►Despite significant efforts and initiatives taken to address climate change over the past 
decade, Manitoba has not achieved any significant reductions in GHG emissions. Beginning in 
2017, however, Manitoba has made noteworthy strides in revitalizing and integrating its efforts 
to address climate change. With the introduction of its Made-in-Manitoba Plan and The 2018 
Climate and Green Plan Act, Manitoba announced its strategy to “lead and innovate” in 
sustainable development by organizing against the four “pillars” of climate, jobs, water and 
nature, pursuant to which it has identified 16 “keystones” for priority action. In addition to 
creating a more comprehensive and integrated framework, Manitoba re-organized its Department 
of Sustainable Development (now “Environment, Climate and Parks”), creating the Climate and 
Green Plan Implementation Office (“CGPIO”) to improve coordination and communications and 
to eliminate a “silo” approach to the province's climate and green initiatives. The CGPIO in turn 
reports to the Expert Advisory Council established under The 2018 Climate and Green Plan Act 
to provide advice and recommendations to the Minister. 
  
►Manitoba's most significant emissions continue to stem from agriculture and 
transportation sectors. In this regard, Manitoba is introducing new initiatives to support 
mitigation strategies including funding opportunities, biofuels and biomass strategies, and the 
introduction of innovative legislation such as The Watershed Districts Act. 
  
►Perhaps the greatest opportunity for emissions reductions generally continues to lie with 
Manitoba Hydro, the Crown-owned utility, and its tremendous potential for the development of 
additional sources of renewable energy for export and the displacement of fossil fuel generated 
power that may result. 
  
►In some respects, Manitoba is fortunate in that its carbon footprint is smaller than might 
be expected due to the availability of non-emitting hydroelectric generators. On the other hand, 
in order to reduce emissions it must continue to innovate in the agriculture and transportation 
sectors. It remains to be seen how Manitoba will achieve significant emissions reductions in 
these sectors, and particularly the agricultural sector, given the new federal blanket requirement 
to achieve a 30% reduction in GHG emissions through the sector's use of nutrients by 2030 in 
contrast to the province's view that not only is nutrient use already being properly managed, any 
reduction in nutrients would lead to lower yields and in turn compromise Manitoba producers 
and consumers as well as jobs and food security. Furthermore, the effects of Manitoba's climate 
and its population distribution should also not be overlooked--cold winters, warm summers and 
long distances to travel typically require higher per capita energy consumption. 
  
►Overall, the Government of Manitoba sees the province as being well positioned to 
capitalize on opportunities associated with climate change initiatives and is advancing its vision 
to be the “cleanest, greenest and most climate resilient province” in Canada.
